registers.role: sample frame, outcomes, covariates and linkage
variables_mentioned: household composition / children residing in the household

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics Denmark published statistics (VIE1: average age of males and females getting married; Nyt fra Danmarks Statistik on births out of wedlock)
registers.role: contextual background figures, not analysis data
variables_mentioned: mean age of first marriage (32.9 for Danish women)
share of first/second/third+ births out of wedlock

linkages: Individual-level register information merged using a unique personal identification number available in the registers
Children linked to the focal individual by residing in the same household at the beginning of the year

Cohabitation status determined from the household/residence of the focal individual at the beginning of the year; a cohabitation is new if the woman is single at the beginning of year t and cohabiting at the beginning of year t+1

sample.universe: All Danish residents in the Danish administrative registers from 1985 onward; the analysis population is unmarried women aged 18 and above resident in Denmark
sample.unit_of_observation: woman-year (annual stocks and flows aggregated into group-specific rates); the decomposition itself operates on population-level rates
selection_rules: Women (corresponding results for men are reported in Online Appendix Figures A2–A5)
Aged 18 and above, because 18 is the age at which marriage is legal in Denmark
Unmarried at the beginning of the year (single or cohabiting): the at-risk-of-marriage population
Same-sex marriages counted once, to avoid a mismatch between numerator and denominator
For the transition rates: single women aged 18+ at the beginning of the year (1st and 2nd transition) or cohabiting women aged 18+ at the beginning of the year (3rd transition)
Children aged 18 and above residing with married or cohabiting adult(s) are included in the risk population as singles, if they are not one of the primary adults in the residence
sample.period: 2003–2018 for the refined marriage rate (Table 1); 2009–2018 for the decompositions with 2008 as the reference year; 2008–2018 for the three transition rates; 2003–2007 for the pre-period robustness decompositions

construction_notes: Refined marriage rate = annual number of new marriages involving women (opposite-sex and same-sex, each same-sex marriage counted once) per 1,000 unmarried women aged 18+ at risk at the beginning of the year
Age measured at the beginning of the year, in six groups: 25 or below, 26–30, 31–35, 36–40, 41–45, above 45 (Figure 2's panel legends print these as '<26', '26-30', '31-35', '35-40', '40-45', '46+')

Income measured as individual disposable income, including social transfers, pensions and investment income; four groups built on the 2008 income quartile thresholds, held fixed so that group sizes vary over time
Children: indicator equal to one if at least one child resides in the same household as the focal individual at the beginning of the year
Marriage history: indicator equal to one if the focal individual has been married previously but is unmarried at the beginning of the year
Employment status: three groups — employed, unemployed, out of the workforce

Das Gupta (1993) decomposition run year-by-year with 2008 as the reference year; Part I reports absolute differences, Part II within-group percentage differences to the group's own 2008 behavioral component
No education covariate is included: the paper argues the income measure captures it, since income and education are highly correlated
Robustness: income groups rebuilt from household equivalized disposable income (Online Appendix Figure A1)

claims.statement: The refined marriage rate for unmarried women aged 18+ in Denmark fell by 9.85 marriages per 1,000 between 2008 and 2011, a 30% decrease.

treatment.label: Calendar year in the wake of the Great Recession (2009-2018), relative to the 2008 reference year

definition.value: Not a manipulated treatment. The paper compares each calendar year t in 2009-2018 with 2008, the year before the onset of the marriage rate decline, which coincides with the onset of the Great Recession in Denmark (systemic banking crisis 2008-2010). Das Gupta's (1993) decomposition is run year-by-year with 2008 as the reference year.

timing.value: Annual; each year t in 2009-2018 is compared with the reference year 2008. Stocks (at-risk populations and covariates) are measured at the beginning of the year T; marriages are counted over the full calendar year t.

outcome.label: Refined marriage rate (new marriages per 1,000 unmarried women aged 18+)

definition.value: Annual number of new marriages involving women, both opposite-sex and same-sex (same-sex marriages counted once), per 1,000 unmarried women aged 18 and above at risk of marriage at the beginning of the year (single or cohabiting).

timing.value: Calendar year t; the at-risk denominator is counted at the beginning of the year.

units.value: marriages per 1,000 unmarried women aged 18+ (difference to the 2008 rate)

magnitude.interpretation: “a 30% decrease” relative to 2008 (the paper's own words)

estimand.target_population: Unmarried women aged 18 and above resident in Denmark
estimand.time_horizon: 2011, i.e. 3 years after the 2008 reference year

population.description: Unmarried (single or cohabiting) women aged 18 and above resident in Denmark
population.selection: Women unmarried and aged 18+ at the beginning of the year (at-risk-of-marriage population)

identification.source_of_variation: None exploited for causal identification: the refined marriage rate is compared across calendar years, with 2008 (the pre-decline year, coinciding with the onset of the Great Recession in Denmark) as the reference.

key_assumptions.assumption: The annual change in the aggregate marriage rate can be written as an additive sum of group-specific behavioral (rate/direct) and compositional (structural/size) components, as in Das Gupta's (1993) standardization and decomposition.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Equations (1)-(3); the paper states that the age group-specific decompositions are shown as absolute differences and sum up to the total marriage rate decline.

formal.as_written: Group specific contribution (not pre.mar.) = (# Marriages, not pre.mar._t / # Unmarried women, not pre.mar_T) * (# Unmarried women, not pre.mar._T / # Unmarried women _T) - (# Marriages, not pre.mar._t=2008 / # Unmar.wom., not pre.mar._T=2008) * (# Unmar. women, not pre.mar._T=2008 / # Unmarried wom._T=2008)

key_assumptions.assumption: Absent the Great Recession the marriage rate would have stayed at its 2008 level, so that a year's difference from 2008 measures the decline in the wake of the recession rather than a continuing pre-existing trend.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 1 shows the Danish rate broadly stable 2003-2007; Online Appendix Figures A19-A23 re-run the decompositions for the pre-period 2003-2007 with 2008 as baseline and show no consistent behavioral or compositional changes.

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis conditions on the at-risk-of-marriage population: women aged 18 and above who are unmarried (single or cohabiting) at the beginning of the year.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The definition of the refined marriage rate in the data section and the note to Table 1.

implies_edges.from: at-risk population: unmarried women aged 18+ at the beginning of the year
implies_edges.to: refined marriage rate (new marriages per 1,000 unmarried women aged 18+)

key_assumptions.assumption: Subgroups of each sociodemographic covariate are mutually exclusive and membership is measured at the beginning of the year, so each woman at risk and each marriage is attributed to exactly one group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The data section states that each of the five covariates is split into mutually exclusive subgroups.

threats_discussed: The paper notes that because the baseline number of new entries into marriage varies by age group, the formal (absolute) decomposition alone cannot establish which age group exhibits the largest behavioral change; Part II of the analysis is introduced for that reason
